questions.q: How many power relationships do most successful people build over a career?
a: Around 12 to 15
Around 3 to 5
Around 25 to 30
Fifty or more
questions.why: Lesson 1 says most successful people have roughly 12 to 15 power relationships throughout their careers.

questions.q: How did Bill Jenkins strengthen his relationship with a key client?
a: He switched from formal presentations to informal chats
He lowered his firm's prices significantly
He sent detailed written reports each week
He hired the client's assistant onto his team
questions.why: Lesson 1 says the client preferred informal conversation, and following that advice made the client one of his biggest.

questions.q: Why does the summary advise building ties with people at a similar stage?
a: People already successful rarely welcome newcomers
Peers are more likely to lend money
Established figures have less time to talk
Similar people share the same weaknesses
questions.why: Lesson 2 says someone who has already succeeded is unlikely to bring a newcomer into their close circle.

questions.q: What is the benefit of connecting with people unlike you?
a: Their strengths can cover what you lack
They are easier to persuade and influence
They rarely compete with you for opportunities
They tend to stay in touch more often
questions.why: Lesson 2 says different people's strengths compensate for your gaps, citing Jobs and Wozniak at Apple.

questions.q: What does the summary say genuine power relationships require?
a: Focusing on helping others rather than using them
Collecting as many contacts as possible
Offering favors only when you need one back
Keeping business and friendship separate
questions.why: Lesson 3 says you should look solely at how you can help others, without calculating what they can do for you.
